Explore stocks on Coinbase

Tech giant Meta this week agreed to pay $17 billion as part of a settlement to end a landmark trial related to safeguards for younger users of social media. It is one of the largest such settlements ever, though it represents only a fraction of the $201 billion in revenue that the company booked last year.

Here's a look at some other notable corporate settlements.

BP and the Deepwater Horizon disaster

Oil giant BP agreed to pay $20 billion for the Deepwater Horizon disaster that became the worst offshore spill in the nation's history.

The settlement, first announced in 2016, included $5.5 billion in civil Clean Water Act penalties and billions more to cover environmental damage and other claims by the five Gulf states and local governments. The money is to be paid out over roughly 16 years.

Enron and its massive accounting scandal

Enron, once the nation's seventh-largest company, filed for bankruptcy protection in 2001, after years of accounting tricks could no longer hide billions of dollars in debt or make failing ventures appear profitable. The energy company's collapse put more than 5,000 people out of work and wiped out more than $2 billion in employee pensions.

Twenty-four Enron executives, including former CEO Jeffrey Skilling, were convicted for their roles in the fraud.

A class-action lawsuit led to the recovery of more than $7 billion in funds.

WorldCom hid falling profits in one of the worst cases of accounting fraud

WorldCom Inc. collapsed and went into bankruptcy in 2002 following revelations of an $11 billion accounting fraud that included pressure from top executives on subordinates to inflate numbers to make the company seem more profitable. The collapse caused losses to stockholders, including those who had invested through retirement plans.

In 2005, the company agreed to pay shareholders about $750 million in cash and stock, while major banks and accounting firms settled for about $6 billion.

WorldCom's former CEO, Bernie Ebbers was convicted in New York in 2005 on securities fraud and other charges and received a 25-year sentence. He died in 2020, just over a month after his early release from prison.

After its collapse, WorldCom reemerged under a new name, MCI. It was taken over by Verizon and relocated its operations to Ashburn, Virginia.

JPMorgan, Bank of America and the housing bets that shook the world

JPMorgan Chase & Co. agreed to pay $13 billion in a landmark settlement in 2013. The firm acknowledged that it misled investors about the quality of risky mortgage-backed securities ahead of the 2008 financial crisis.

title: Why Meta Platforms Stock Popped Today

Why Meta Platforms Stock Popped Today
Danny Vena, CPA, The Motley Fool

Shares of Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) rallied Thursday morning, gaining as much as 4.1%. As of 11:46 a.m. ET, the stock was still up 1.9%.

The catalyst that sent the social media and artificial intelligence (AI) specialist higher was news that the company had settled a high-profile court case.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
It could have been much worse

News broke Wednesday morning that Meta had reached a far-reaching legal settlement with 47 states, the District of Columbia (D.C.), and U.S. territories. The case involved allegations that the company had endangered children's mental health by purposefully making its social media platforms addictive. The suit also claimed Meta violated various consumer protection laws by collecting data from children under the age of 13.

Meta has agreed to pay up to $16.7 billion, to be divided among the various states and territories, with equal payments over the next 10 years. The company reached a separate settlement with Texas for up to $1 billion. Meta will also institute default safeguards to prevent minors from using the platform at night and mute notifications during school hours.

The potential outcome in the case could have been much worse for Meta, as some commentators suggested the maximum fine could have been as much as $1.4 trillion -- equaling the total amount of the company's market cap. Moreover, a previous case in New Mexico was decided against Meta, with the judge ordering the company to pay $567 million over charges that its social media platforms fueled a "current mental health crisis among New Mexico's youth."

The company generated revenue of $60.8 billion in the second quarter, so Meta is paying out roughly 25 days' worth of revenue. Looked at another way, the company has about 2.6 million shares outstanding, which works out to roughly $6.51 per share, just slightly more than Meta's Q2 profit of $6.18 per share.

The settlement of this high-profile case removes a big overhang from Meta's stock, which has languished in recent years. And at 22 times earnings, savvy investors can pick up shares at a discount.

Settlement Resolves the Trial at a Fraction of Claimed Damages

The Meta deal resolves allegations that Facebook and Instagram were designed to encourage compulsive use among children and teens and that Meta misled users about platform safety. Payments run in annual installments over 10 years, with California potentially receiving $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion. Participating states receive 70% of the allocated payment, while the remaining 30%, or $5.3 billion, is released only if YouTube and TikTok implement the same age assurance measures and match that amount.

All three major US stock indexes were down slightly in late-morning trading Wednesday, as market participants took in the latest inflation data and prepared for Nvidia (NVDA) to release its earnings results after markets close.

The personal consumption expenditures index, a measure of inflation, rose by 0.2% in July, faster than the 0.1% gain expected in a survey conducted by Bloomberg as of 6:10 am ET and following a 0.1% drop in June. The July figure keeps the year-over-year rate at 3.7%. The core PCE index, which excludes food and energy prices, increased by 0.2%, as expected and following a 0.1% gain in June. The year-over-year rate remained at 3.3% in the month.

Separately, US gross domestic product rose by 1.5% in Q2, unrevised from the advance estimate released last month and matching the consensus estimate from a Bloomberg survey as of 6:10 am ET.

In company news, Meta Platforms (META) has agreed to pay a maximum of $16.68 billion to resolve claims brought by several US states that the tech giant used its platforms to "ensnare" youth and teens, according to a Wednesday filing in federal court. The consent agreement's injunctive relief also requires Meta to take several steps to regulate children's usage of its social media platforms, including daily limits and nighttime blocks. In a separate release, Meta said the agreement includes a payment of about $18 billion to be distributed in annual installments over a 10-year period. Plaintiff states will receive about $12.7 billion over the decade, while the remaining roughly 30%, or $5.3 billion, will be released if Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) YouTube and TikTok "implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode, and Age assurance measures," and they each pay an amount equal to the 30% figure. Meta shares were up 2.1% around midday. Alphabet's Class C and Class A shares were down 1.1% and 1.2%, respectively.

Victory Capital (VCTR) signed a definitive agreement to acquire First Eagle Investments from Genstar Capital and First Eagle employees for about $7 billion, Victory said Wednesday. Victory will pay about $4.4 billion in cash, $2 billion in newly issued shares and will assume $575 million of First Eagle's existing 7.25% senior secured notes due 2032, the company said. The deal is expected to close in Q1 2027, at which point Genstar will own a 14.6% stake in Victory, the company said. Victory Capital shares were up 6.3%.

Intuit (INTU) reported fiscal Q4 adjusted earnings late Tuesday of $4.03 per diluted share, up from $2.75 a year earlier and above the FactSet consensus of $3.58. Fiscal Q4 revenue was $4.35 billion, up from $3.83 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $4.27 billion. For fiscal Q1, the company expects adjusted EPS of $2.44 to $2.48 on revenue of $4.29 billion to $4.31 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet expect $4.04 and $4.35 billion, respectively. For fiscal 2027, Intuit expects adjusted EPS of $22.88 to $23.12 on revenue of $23.28 billion to $23.51 billion. Analysts expect $27.34 and $23.70 billion, respectively. The company raised its quarterly dividend to $1.38 per share from $1.20, payable on Oct. 16. Intuit shares were down 4.5%.

Boston Scientific (BSX) identified a cybersecurity incident that affected some of its IT systems and led to global disruptions in operations, the company said Wednesday in a regulatory filing. Boston Scientific shares were down 4.7%.

Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet's Google are in talks with Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI over revenue-sharing deals for hosting Moonshot's Kimi K3 model, Reuters reported Wednesday, citing sources familiar with the matter. Separately, Amazon plans to expand fulfillment capacity, same-day delivery and its logistics network in Canada despite escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada, Business Insider reported Wednesday, citing internal company documents. Lastly, Amazon's AWS unit is acquiring DuckLabs, the Amsterdam-based company behind the open-source analytical database DuckDB, for an undisclosed sum, Amazon said. The deal is expected to close shortly, Amazon said. Shares of Amazon were down 0.6%, and Microsoft was up 0.7%.

title: Meta agrees to new protections for teenagers in US in 18bn dollar settlement
detail:
Meta agrees to new protections for teenagers in US in 18bn dollar settlement
Meta agrees to new protections for teenagers in US in 18bn dollar settlement · PA Media: Money
Anna Wise, Press Association Business Reporter
Wed, August 26, 2026 at 11:18 AM EDT 2 min read
META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Facebook and Instagram owner Meta has agreed to pay up to 18 billion US dollars (£13.3 billion) as part of a settlement ending a legal battle in the US, where it will also introduce major new protections for teenage users.

The agreement resolves claims filed by 47 US states accusing the tech giant of designing Instagram with features that are addictive to children and teenagers and can harm their mental health.

It brings an end to a trial that kicked off last week in California and that had expected to see chief executive Mark Zuckerberg give evidence before a jury in federal court.

The settlement is viewed as one of the largest in state consumer protection history in the US.

Jay Jones, the attorney general for Virginia, said: "For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health."

He said the settlement would "put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm".

Meta unveiled a set of new protections and controls that will automatically apply to under-18s on Instagram and Facebook, subject to court approval and only for participating US states.

This includes a default night-time block, between midnight and 6am, muting notifications during school hours, hiding the number of "likes" and reactions on posts by default, and blocking teens from using extreme makeup filters.

Meta has also committed to strengthening tools to prevent underage accounts being created and protecting teenagers from harmful content.

These new measures will not apply to users worldwide, including the UK.

The total settlement will be made in instalments over 10 years to the US states involved.

But Meta called on rival social media platforms TikTok and YouTube to make similar changes to restrict teenage usage.

It warned that 30% of the settlement, amounting to about 5.2 billion dollars (£3.8 billion), would only be paid if YouTube and TikTok agreed to pay the same sum, and if they implement one-hour daily limits, night mode and age-assurance measures.

Meta's chief legal office CJ Mahoney said its new protections for teenagers "will only work if all our peers join us".

"Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution," he said.

"As a parent, I'm proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new ground-breaking agreement.

"But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta's lead."

Meta settled a case this morning that management had flagged as potentially material, and the stock barely moved. Twenty-nine state attorneys general dropped their federal trial in Oakland after roughly a week and a half of testimony in exchange for a payment reported by Reuters, Forbes and BNN Bloomberg at $16.68 billion, one of the largest state-AG settlements ever extracted from a technology company. By 10:25 a.m. ET, Meta (NASDAQ:META) was changing hands at $570.04, a fraction of a cent below Tuesday's $570.05 close. Jim Cramer, posting live on X, called it "one hated stock.. i mean like despised.". The market was still open as this went to press.

24/7 Wall St.
META Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
What The 29 States Alleged

The complaint accused Meta of designing Instagram and Facebook to be addictive to young users, misrepresenting platform safety, and unlawfully collecting data from children under 13 in violation of the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. California, Colorado, New Jersey and Kentucky served as lead plaintiffs. The federal trial opened around Aug. 17 to 18 before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers and was in its second week when the two sides reached terms. Meta denied wrongdoing, and the agreement reportedly requires all parties to waive appeal rights once final judgment is entered.

Settlement Size Remains Unclear

Reported totals range from NBC's "up to $16 billion" to Variety's "up to $18 billion," with CNBC, Quartz and Yahoo Finance at $16.7 billion and CBS at $17 billion. The recurring "up to" phrasing suggests a structure with contingencies rather than a single lump sum. The settlement also carries operational strings: daily time caps for teen users on Facebook and Instagram, overnight usage restrictions, enhanced age-verification systems, and expanded parental controls.

Cramer's Take

At 9:27 a.m. ET, Cramer posted: "Meta was looking at a trillion; betting like was $200 billion and big restrictions: final is $12.6b and no onerous restrictions". Mainstream reporting does not support that early read. The $12.6 billion figure sits well below major outlets' numbers, and the operational restrictions are onerous by any fair reading.
